paragraphs.heading: What the theory says
paragraphs.text: The Big Bang is a physical theory of how the universe grew out of an early state that was very dense and very hot. Running the expansion backward with the known laws of physics leads to an extremely hot, dense early universe. Models built on this idea account for many things we observe: how common the light elements are, the cosmic microwave background (CMB), the redshifted light of galaxies, and how the universe is arranged on the largest scales. A wide range of evidence strongly favours the model, and it is now widely accepted.

paragraphs.heading: From inflation to galaxies
paragraphs.text: The original model traced the universe back toward a singularity. The modern view adds cosmic inflation, a phase of speeded-up expansion in the earliest moments, out of which the universe came in a supercooled state. A reheating event then turned the energy that powered inflation into a hot, dense plasma, which set off the hot Big Bang. As the universe expanded, it cooled enough for subatomic particles to form, and later atoms. These first elements, mostly hydrogen with some helium and lithium, were pulled together by gravity, helped by dark matter, into early stars and galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: How the idea took shape
paragraphs.text: Alexander Friedmann introduced the idea of an expanding universe in 1922, when he derived the Friedmann equations. In 1929 Edwin Hubble published the earliest observation of the expansion, now called Hubble's law: galaxies are moving away from Earth, and the farther they are, the faster they go. Working apart from both men, Georges Lemaître proposed in 1931 that the universe came from a primeval atom, which introduced the modern Big Bang idea. In 1964 the CMB was found by accident, and measurements over the next few years showed it was the same in every direction and had an energy curve that fit a hot, dense past. By the late 1960s most cosmologists were sure the rival steady-state model was wrong.

paragraphs.heading: Three working assumptions
paragraphs.text: The models rest on three main assumptions. The first is that the laws of physics hold everywhere. The second, called the cosmological principle, says the universe, viewed at large scales, is homogeneous and isotropic, meaning it looks the same in every direction wherever you stand. The third is that matter can be treated as a perfect fluid, one with no viscosity and with pressure in proportion to density. These started as postulates but have since been tested: the fine-structure constant has shifted by at most about 10⁻⁵ over much of the universe's age, and CMB temperatures confirm the cosmological principle to a level of 10⁻⁵.

paragraphs.heading: What the universe is made of
paragraphs.text: In Big Bang cosmology, the density of mass and energy decides the shape of the universe and how it changes. Putting observations together with thermodynamics and particle physics, cosmologists have traced what that density consists of across cosmic history. Today, luminous matter such as stars and planets is less than 5% of it. Dark matter accounts for 27%, and dark energy for the remaining 68%.

paragraphs.heading: Horizons in both directions
paragraphs.text: A key feature of the Big Bang picture is the presence of horizons. The universe has a finite age and light moves at a finite speed, so light from some past events may not have reached Earth yet, which limits how far away we can see. Going the other way, space is expanding and distant objects are moving off ever faster, so light sent out today may never catch up with them. That sets a future horizon, a limit on which future events we can affect. Supernova redshifts show the expansion is speeding up, which is put down to dark energy, and if that goes on there is a future horizon too.

paragraphs.heading: What is still unexplained
paragraphs.text: Some features of the observed universe are not yet well explained by the Big Bang models. These include why matter and antimatter exist in unequal amounts, known as baryon asymmetry. They also include the detailed nature of the dark matter around galaxies and where dark energy comes from.
